McLaren: McLaren has tweaked the rear‑corner airflow by reshaping the brake‑duct opening, which helps the brakes stay cooler and lets the car run a bit more consistently through fast corners. They’ve also added an “alternative straight‑line” flap setting on the rear wing, trimming drag so the car can hit higher top speeds on the longest sections of the circuit. Together, these changes should give McLaren better stability under braking and a speed boost on the straights, key factors for gaining positions this weekend.
Mercedes F1 Team: Mercedes has tweaked the front‑suspension fairings, sharpening their angle to clean up the airflow around the car’s front wheels, which should give a bit more grip and stability into the corners. They’ve also narrowed the rear exit on the engine cover to improve cooling efficiency, helping the power unit stay in its optimal temperature window for longer stints. Together, these changes aim to keep the car balanced and fast over the whole weekend, especially on the high‑speed sections.
Racing Bulls / RB: Racing Bulls has reshaped the car’s side‑pod inlet and matching engine‑cover panels to smooth airflow and stop the occasional cooling hiccup that has plagued recent outings, giving the team a more reliable power‑unit on a hot weekend. At the back, the floor, diffuser, rear‑wing pylons and exhaust have been tweaked and lowered, while the rear‑suspension fairings and winglets have been re‑profiled, all to tighten the car’s rear grip and boost straight‑line thrust. In short, the updates should keep the car cooler, more stable through fast corners and stronger on the long straights, which could translate into a solid points haul this race.
Scuderia Ferrari: Ferrari has reshaped the front wing’s endplates, adding a fresh dive‑plane and re‑positioned foot‑vane pieces to tighten the airflow and give the car a bit more bite out of the corners. They’ve also stripped out the central piece of the rear‑venturi “tail” and slimmed down the mirror stalk, which cleans up the rear‑end flow and reduces drag. Finally, the floor now carries a single, streamlined vertical element that helps keep the car planted, giving the team a small but valuable edge for the upcoming weekend.
Aston Martin: Aston Martin did not submit any updates for this event.
Haas F1 Team: Haas has tweaked the front‑corner aerodynamics, adding a new flow‑conditioning element that smooths the air and gives a little extra down‑force where the car needs it most. At the same time, the cooling louvers on that same area have been re‑shaped for the specific temperature demands of this circuit, helping the engine stay in the sweet spot without sacrificing grip. Together, the changes should give the car a tighter front end and more reliable power delivery over the weekend’s laps.
Audi F1 Team: Audi’s F1 car gets a fresh set of aero tweaks – a reshaped front‑wing endplate, a re‑worked lower deflector at the front and rear corners, and a new lower beam wing – plus a revised rear floor, suspension and rear wing. These changes tighten the airflow and boost down‑force where it counts, giving the car more grip and stability through the high‑speed corners of this weekend’s circuit. In short, the updates should make the Audi quicker out of the bends and more consistent over a race distance.
Alpine F1 Team: Alpine has rolled out a completely new front wing – together with fresh endplates and a re‑shaped nose – to give the car a tighter front grip and a more stable feel into the first corners. The revised front‑corner geometry smooths the airflow around the car’s side pods, while a small winglet added to the diffuser boosts rear down‑force without adding drag. In short, the package should make the car stick to the tarmac better and give the drivers a bigger window to attack on this weekend’s circuit.
Cadillac: Cadillac’s new package widens and reshapes the side‑pod inlets, re‑profiles the engine‑cover fins and freshens the top‑deck louvers, giving the car a bigger “breathing” window so the engine stays cooler and can push harder without overheating. The under‑cut around the side‑pod “coke” area, new mirror‑stay angles and re‑shaped roll‑hoop leg fairings clean up the airflow, tightening the car’s front‑end balance for more predictable turn‑in. Finally, a re‑worked floor‑bib, leading‑edge floor strips, diffuser and beam‑wing all add a little extra downforce where it counts, translating into better traction off the line and through the corners for this weekend’s sprint.
